nameStory: Swamp beggarticks gets its name from two distinct features: it loves wet, swampy places, and its seeds are notorious "beggars" that stick to anything passing by. The tiny seeds have barbed tips that grab onto fur, feathers, and clothing like desperate hitchhikers pleading for a ride to new territory.
description: Swamp beggarticks is a modest annual wildflower that thrives in New England's wetlands and marshy areas. This member of the sunflower family grows 1-3 feet tall with branching stems and opposite leaves. Unlike many of its flashy relatives, it produces small, inconspicuous yellowish flower heads without the showy petals you'd expect from the daisy family. Its real claim to fame comes later in the season when it produces sticky seeds that seem magnetically attracted to anyone walking through wet meadows.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, yellow disc flowers clustered in heads about 1/4 inch across with no showy petals - just the tiny tubular center flowers that look like miniature buttons

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves that are lance-shaped with toothed edges, feeling slightly rough when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Flattened, brown seeds topped with 2-4 barbed bristles that grab onto clothing and fur with surprising tenacity - you'll feel them sticking to your pants

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Branching annual that forms loose colonies in wet areas, with multiple stems arising from the base creating a somewhat bushy appearance

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Almost always found with its feet wet - in marshes, swamp edges, and seasonally flooded areas where the soil feels squishy underfoot

habitat: Swamp beggarticks lives up to its name by inhabiting New England's wettest places - marshes, swamp margins, pond edges, and seasonally flooded meadows. You'll find it in areas where the soil stays consistently moist or even waterlogged, often growing alongside sedges, cattails, and other water-loving plants. It thrives in both full sun and partial shade as long as its roots can stay wet.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in wet soil as temperatures warm, with young plants emerging as small rosettes of toothed leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly and begin blooming in mid to late summer with their small, buttonlike flower heads appearing at stem tips.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming continues into early fall, followed quickly by seed production - this is when those notorious hitchhiker seeds become a real nuisance to hikers.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist above ice and snow, but the annual plant has completed its life cycle, leaving only seeds to survive until spring.

funFact: A single swamp beggarticks plant can produce over 1,000 seeds, each equipped with barbed hooks so effective that they inspired the invention of Velcro - Swiss engineer George de Mestral got the idea after pulling countless beggarticks seeds from his dog's fur after a walk.
confusionNotes: With 14 beggarticks species in New England, identification can be tricky! The key distinguishing feature is the lack of showy ray petals (the "daisy petals") that many of its relatives possess. Remember: "swamp beggarticks keeps it simple" - just yellow button centers, no fancy petals, always in wet places.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - beggarticks aren't actually ticks at all, but plant seeds that stick just as persistently. The "beggarticks" name comes from their habit of begging for rides by clinging to passersby, while "ticks" refers to their small size and tenacious grip, not the blood-sucking arachnids.
compareHints: Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays. It's also more consistently found in truly wet conditions than devil's beggarticks, which tolerates drier soils. The small, simple flower heads distinguish it from the larger, showier tickseed sunflower.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower).

Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant.
Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems.

Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats.

Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely).

Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments.
Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions.
Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils.
White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals.
